intro.title: Random samples
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Statistics is about learning from a **sample**: a few values drawn from something bigger. R can draw random samples itself, which is a great way to see how much results wobble from sample to sample.

`sample(x, size)` picks `size` values from `x`. Without `replace = TRUE` each value can be picked only once, like drawing names from a hat; with it, values can repeat, like rolling a die:

```
sample(1:20, 5)                      # five different numbers
sample(1:6, 10, replace = TRUE)      # ten dice rolls
```

Random numbers are different every run. To get the **same** "random" numbers again, so a result can be checked or shared, set the starting point first with `set.seed()`. Any whole number works; the same seed always gives the same draws:

```
set.seed(7)
sample(1:6, 3, replace = TRUE)
```

R can also draw from the classic shapes: `runif(n, min, max)` gives numbers spread evenly between two limits, and `rnorm(n, mean, sd)` gives numbers from a **normal** (bell-shaped) distribution, most of them near the mean.

A **simulation** repeats an experiment many times. `replicate(1000, expr)` runs `expr` 1000 times and collects the results, so you can see how results spread out.

intro.title: The normal distribution
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Many measurements, such as weights of loaves, heights of seedlings or errors in a reading, pile up in a **bell shape** around their mean. That shape is the **normal distribution**, and it is described by two numbers: the mean (the centre) and the standard deviation (the spread).

For any normal distribution, about **68%** of values are within 1 sd of the mean, about **95%** within 2 sd, and almost all within 3 sd.

Say a bakery's loaves weigh on average 500 g with sd 6 g. R answers questions about it with two functions:

| Function | Question | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pnorm(q, mean, sd)` | What share is **below** q? | `pnorm(490, 500, 6)` is about 0.048 |
| `qnorm(p, mean, sd)` | Below which value is a share p? | `qnorm(0.95, 500, 6)` is about 509.9 |

For "above", take the rest: `1 - pnorm(510, 500, 6)`. For "between", subtract: `pnorm(510, 500, 6) - pnorm(490, 500, 6)`.

A **z-score** says how many sds a value is from the mean: `(x - mean) / sd`. A 488 g loaf has z = (488 − 500) / 6 = −2. Without a mean and sd, `pnorm(z)` uses the standard normal (mean 0, sd 1).

```
pnorm(490, mean = 500, sd = 6)     # share of loaves under 490 g
qnorm(0.95, mean = 500, sd = 6)    # 95% of loaves weigh less than this
```

intro.title: Correlation
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Do students who revise more score higher? A **correlation** measures how closely two numeric columns move together, as one number from −1 to 1:

| r | Means |
| --- | --- |
| near 1 | When one is high, the other is high (a strong positive link) |
| near 0 | No straight-line link |
| near −1 | When one is high, the other is low (a strong negative link) |

```
study <- data.frame(
  student = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli", "Fay", "Gus", "Hal"),
  hours = c(2, 5, 1, 4, 6, 3, 7, 2),
  phone = c(5, 2, 6, 2, 1, 4, 1, 3),
  sleep = c(7, 8, 6, 7, 8, 9, 7, 6),
  score = c(64, 71, 52, 75, 79, 58, 84, 62)
)
cor(study$hours, study$score)    # 0.93: strongly positive
cor(study$phone, study$score)    # -0.91: strongly negative
```

`cor()` on a whole table of numbers gives every pair at once, as a matrix: `cor(study[, c("hours", "phone", "sleep", "score")])`.

`cor()` measures **straight-line** links, and one unusual value can pull it a long way. `method = "spearman"` uses ranks instead, so it is less affected by outliers.

And the big warning: **correlation is not causation**. Revising and phone use are linked (r = −0.91), so either could be behind the scores, or something else behind both. A correlation tells you two things go together, not why.

intro.title: Confidence intervals
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A trading-standards officer weighs 10 loaves from the bakery. Their mean is 495.8 g, but a different 10 loaves would give a different mean. How far from the **true** mean of all the loaves could 495.8 be?

```
loaf <- c(497, 503, 491, 499, 488, 502, 495, 494, 500, 489)
mean(loaf)    # 495.8
```

The **standard error** measures how much a sample mean wobbles: `sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))`. Bigger samples have smaller standard errors.

A **95% confidence interval** is a range built so that, for 95% of samples, it contains the true mean. For a mean it is roughly the mean ± 2 standard errors; exactly, the 2 is `qt(0.975, df = n - 1)`, which allows for small samples.

R works it out with `t.test()`. The result holds many parts; `$conf.int` is the interval and `$estimate` the mean:

```
t.test(loaf)$conf.int    # 492.0 to 499.6
```

`conf.level = 0.90` gives a 90% interval, which is narrower: being less sure buys a tighter range. To read the interval: we are 95% confident the true mean weight is between 492.0 g and 499.6 g. Notice that 500 g, the label, is **outside** it.

intro.title: Testing a claim
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The bakery's label says 500 g, and the 10 loaves averaged 495.8 g. Is that just luck of the sample, or are the loaves really light? A **hypothesis test** answers in a careful way:

First, assume the claim is true: the true mean is 500 g. This is the **null hypothesis**. Then work out how surprising the data would be if it were. That surprise is the **p-value**: the chance of a sample mean at least this far from 500 just by luck.

The **one-sample t-test** does all of it. `mu` is the claimed mean:

```
loaf <- c(497, 503, 491, 499, 488, 502, 495, 494, 500, 489)
t.test(loaf, mu = 500)$p.value    # 0.034
```

A small p-value means the data would be surprising if the claim were true. By a common convention, **p < 0.05** counts as evidence against the claim, often called "statistically significant". Here p = 0.034, so the data are evidence that the loaves weigh less than 500 g on average.

A large p-value does **not** prove the claim; it only means the data don't give clear evidence against it. Small samples often can't tell.

By default the test is two-sided: too heavy and too light both count. If only one direction matters, say so: `alternative = "less"` tests whether the true mean is below `mu`.

intro.title: Comparing two groups
intro.bodyMarkdown:
In the seedling trial, the leaf-compost trays averaged 10.6 cm and the peat trays 8.2 cm. With only four trays each, could that gap be luck? The **two-sample t-test** asks: if both composts really gave the same mean height, how surprising would a gap this big be?

```
seedlings <- data.frame(
  tray = 1:12,
  compost = c("peat", "peat", "peat", "peat", "leaf", "leaf", "leaf", "leaf", "home", "home", "home", "home"),
  height_cm = c(8.2, 7.5, 9.1, 8.0, 10.4, 11.2, 9.8, 10.9, 7.1, 12.8, 6.9, 7.6),
  leaves = c(6, 5, 7, 6, 8, 9, 7, 8, 5, 9, 4, 5)
)
two <- seedlings[seedlings$compost %in% c("peat", "leaf"), ]
t.test(height_cm ~ compost, data = two)
```

The `~` is a **formula**: "height explained by compost". The column on the left is the measurement, the one on the right says which group each row is in, and it must have exactly two groups, so here we first keep only peat and leaf.

The result gives a p-value (0.002: strong evidence of a real difference), the two group means in `$estimate`, and in `$conf.int` a confidence interval for the **difference** between them: leaf minus peat, because the groups are taken in alphabetical order.

R uses the **Welch** version by default, which doesn't assume the two groups are equally spread. That is a safe default.

When each value in one group has a partner in the other, such as the same student's first and second test, use a **paired** test on the two columns: `t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)`. It tests whether the average change is zero.

intro.title: Counts and categories
intro.bodyMarkdown:
t-tests compare means. When the data are **categories**, such as hot lunch or packed lunch, you compare **counts** instead. The school canteen asked 100 students in two years what they usually have:

```
lunch <- data.frame(
  year = rep(c("Y7", "Y8"), c(45, 55)),
  choice = c(rep(c("hot", "packed"), c(30, 15)), rep(c("hot", "packed"), c(20, 35)))
)
tab <- table(lunch$year, lunch$choice)
tab
```

Year 7 chose hot lunch 30 times out of 45, Year 8 only 20 out of 55. Is lunch choice linked to year, or could a split like this happen by chance? The **chi-squared test of independence** compares the counts with what you would **expect** if year made no difference:

```
chisq.test(tab)             # p = 0.005
chisq.test(tab)$expected    # the counts if there were no link
```

The test adds up how far each observed count is from its expected count. Here p = 0.005, so the data are strong evidence that lunch choice differs between the years. (For a 2 × 2 table R applies a small correction by default, which makes the test a little more careful.)

When you only have the counts, not the rows, build the table yourself: `matrix(c(30, 20, 15, 35), nrow = 2)` makes a 2 × 2 grid, filled **column by column**, so its first column is 30 and 20. `chisq.test()` accepts it just like a table. (The Reshaping quest covers matrices properly.)

A **goodness-of-fit** test checks counts in one set of categories against expected shares. Are these 120 dice rolls fair? `chisq.test(c(15, 22, 18, 25, 17, 23))` tests against equal shares; add `p = c(...)` for other expected shares.

The test needs reasonably large counts. If expected counts are below about 5, R warns that the approximation may be incorrect.

intro.title: Linear regression
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A correlation says revision and scores move together. **Linear regression** goes further: it finds the straight line that best fits the points, so you can say **how much** the score goes up per hour and **predict** scores.

```
study <- data.frame(
  student = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli", "Fay", "Gus", "Hal"),
  hours = c(2, 5, 1, 4, 6, 3, 7, 2),
  phone = c(5, 2, 6, 2, 1, 4, 1, 3),
  sleep = c(7, 8, 6, 7, 8, 9, 7, 6),
  score = c(64, 71, 52, 75, 79, 58, 84, 62)
)
model <- lm(score ~ hours, data = study)
coef(model)
```

`lm()` means "linear model", with the same formula as before: score explained by hours. `coef()` gives the line's two numbers: the **intercept** (50.1, the predicted score for 0 hours) and the **slope** (4.8, the extra points per hour of revision). So the line is: score = 50.1 + 4.8 × hours.

**R²** (R-squared), from `summary(model)$r.squared`, says what share of the variation in scores the line explains: 0.86 here, which is a lot. It is the correlation squared.

`predict()` uses the line for new values. It needs a data frame with the same column name:

```
predict(model, newdata = data.frame(hours = 4.5))    # about 71.7
```

Two warnings. Predicting far outside the data (`hours = 20`) trusts the straight line where you have never seen it; that is **extrapolation**, and it can give nonsense like a score over 100. And as with correlation, a good fit is not proof that one thing causes the other.

`residuals(model)` are the gaps between each real score and the line: positive if the student did better than the line predicts.

challenges.solution:
kiosk <- data.frame(
  day = 1:12,
  temp = c(14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 19, 23, 27),
  sales = c(118, 152, 141, 196, 183, 240, 231, 292, 284, 170, 221, 248)
)
model <- lm(sales ~ temp, data = kiosk)
odd_day <- kiosk$day[which.max(abs(residuals(model)))]
